title: Impact measurement: Sample balance does not remove attrition
desc: Examines validity checks for AI experiments and labour surveys, distinguishing credible design from substantive productivity or employment findings.

kps.k: This cluster concerns the credibility of AI-impact measurement, not evidence that AI raises productivity, narrows education gaps or changes employment.
kps.d: The supplied passages document experimental comparability, attrition, survey selection and measurement validation. They provide methodological context for interpreting impact estimates but do not supply those estimates. No substantive disagreement about AI’s effects appears here; the central qualification is that reassuring design checks do not themselves establish an effect or its absence.

kps.k: Experimental comparisons show broad baseline similarity, with individual imbalances that qualify the aggregate picture.
kps.d: In Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps?, joint balance tests find no statistically detectable differences initially or among completers (p=0.172 and 0.616). Yet the initial treatment group has a 6.3-percentage-point lower high-school-only share (p=0.003). Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence reports similar first-task completion times (26.22 versus 26.59 minutes) and grades (3.72 versus 3.89 out of seven). These descriptive comparisons neither prove group equivalence nor establish an AI treatment effect.

kps.k: Attrition checks address differential completion, but substantial non-completion remains an interpretive limit.
kps.d: The education-gap experiment retains 612 control and 562 treatment participants from initial groups of 922 and 873. The authors cannot reject equal completion rates across treatment-by-education groups (p=0.531). Completer comparisons also show no jointly significant baseline differences within education groups, although low-education completers are about 0.9 years younger. The authors suggest that demanding job-like tasks explain relatively high non-completion; they do not demonstrate that explanation. Readers should distinguish failure to detect differential attrition from proof that dropout introduces no bias.

kps.k: Education classifications and labor-market differences constrain interpretations of education-based productivity gaps.
kps.d: The education-gap experiment’s groups have similar age and gender profiles but differ in employment and experience: employee shares are 63.3% versus 75.4%, and average work experience is 10.3 versus 11.6 years. Both groups include participants with incomplete postsecondary studies. The authors report robustness to three alternative education definitions, but the supplied passage gives no corresponding effect estimates. The checks address sensitivity to classification without establishing that education alone explains any productivity difference.

qs.q: In Section 7, we show that our results are robust to dropping participants with incomplete postsecondary education, defining high education as having any postsecondary education (regardless of com- pletion), or restricting the high-education group to participants who completed their postsecondary studies.
qs.a: Does Generative AI Narrow Education-Based Productivity Gaps? Evidence from a Randomized Experiment · Academia · 2026

kps.k: The labor-market survey combines several selection and validation checks, each with a specific scope.
kps.d: Large Language Models, Small Labor Market Effects, revised as Still Waters, Rapid Currents, invited 115,000 workers in each November 2023 and November 2024 round and links eligible completed responses to administrative records. The authors report observable similarity between respondents and survey populations, and between complete and partial respondents before dropout. Randomly offering larger participation prizes increases participation without systematic response differences; reported occupations match registers for 87% of respondents. These checks support the authors’ methodological case, but observable balance does not establish balance on unobserved traits, and occupational agreement does not validate every survey measure.

kps.k: Sampling changes can produce apparent demographic shifts, so comparisons across survey rounds require attention to occupational composition.
kps.d: The labor-market study attributes changing aggregate female representation to a 2023 protocol that randomly invited only half the relevant workers at some workplaces, altering occupations’ weights. Gender composition remained virtually unchanged within occupations and in the unweighted worker population. The authors argue that occupation fixed effects address the compositional change and note that nearly all analyses use the unaffected 2024 round. The practical implication is to separate sampling-induced shifts from changes in the underlying workforce before interpreting trends.

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition that sample-balance and validation checks strengthen the credibility of AI-impact research but do not establish substantive productivity or employment effects, nor eliminate attrition and selection concerns. Across the sources, the common approach is to delimit what the evidence can show: baseline treatment–control comparisons are descriptive; survey representativeness is assessed only on observable characteristics and available pre-dropout responses; and failure to detect differential completion is not proof that non-completion causes no bias. Material variation lies in the particular validity problem addressed. The labour-market survey uses population comparisons, participation-incentive variation and administrative-record validation; one productivity experiment supplies mainly descriptive group comparisons; and the education-gap experiment most directly exposes the residual attrition limitation through substantial sample loss despite statistically reassuring completion tests and broadly balanced completer samples. Individual baseline differences and differences between education groups further qualify aggregate balance findings. These sources therefore reinforce, rather than extend or contest, the synthesis’s central methodological distinction between credible design checks and evidence of AI’s effects.

elens.an: The supplied 2023–2024 source supports the proposition’s core methodological distinction, but only on sample comparability rather than attrition. It reports treatment–control characteristics and first-task outcomes as descriptive statistics, with similar averages for completion time, grade, job satisfaction and self-efficacy. Its explanation of the difference-in-means column and significance thresholds further frames these figures as balance checks, not estimates of AI’s productivity effect. Thus, the source aligns with the cluster’s warning that reassuring design checks do not themselves establish an effect or its absence. Materially, however, this excerpt provides no evidence about completion or dropout, so it cannot independently support the proposition’s specific claim that sample balance does not eliminate attrition concerns. No internal disagreement appears within the supplied evidence; the principal variation is one of scope.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that sample-balance and validation checks strengthen the credibility of AI-impact measurement without eliminating attrition or establishing substantive labour-market effects. It reports that respondents resemble the survey populations on observed characteristics and that complete and partial respondents are similar on recorded characteristics and answers given before dropout. These checks address observable selection and response quality, but they cannot establish balance on unobserved traits or show that dropout is harmless. The source also offers distinct, narrower checks—random incentive variation, administrative validation of reported occupations, and an explanation for sampling-induced shifts in aggregate gender composition. These reinforce the study’s methodological case while varying materially in scope: incentive comparisons concern participation selection, registry agreement validates occupation reporting only, and occupation fixed effects address a particular cross-round compositional change. None independently validates every survey measure or demonstrates an AI effect. This assessment concerns the supplied source, not the prevalence of this view among 2025 publications.

elens.an: The 2026 source supports the proposition that credible balance and attrition checks strengthen an AI experiment’s design but do not eliminate attrition concerns or establish substantive productivity effects. It reports no statistically detectable joint baseline differences among completers and no detected difference in completion rates across treatment-by-education cells. Material qualifications remain: completion fell from 1,795 initial participants to 1,174 completers; some individual education measures were imbalanced; low-education completers differed in age from non-completers; and the proposed explanation that demanding tasks caused non-completion is suggestive rather than demonstrated. Its reported robustness to alternative education definitions is also not accompanied in the supplied material by effect estimates. These limitations qualify rather than contradict the methodological proposition, and the source provides no evidence here that AI raises productivity or narrows education-based gaps.
